title: Tshechu Etiquette: How to Watch a Bhutan Festival
meta_description: How to watch a Bhutanese tshechu well: what the masked dances mean, the dawn thongdrel, what to wear, where to sit, photo rules and when to book hotels.
summary: A tshechu is a religious festival held around the tenth day of a lunar month to honour Guru Rinpoche, with masked cham dances in a dzong courtyard. Visitors are welcome. Dress as for a dzong, sit where locals show you, never step into the dance ground, skip flash, and book hotels months ahead. Dates follow the lunar calendar.

sections.heading: What a tshechu is
paras: Tshechu means 'tenth day' in Dzongkha. These festivals are held in districts across Bhutan on or around the tenth day of a month in the lunar calendar, and they honour Guru Rinpoche, also called Padmasambhava, the 8th-century master who Bhutanese tradition credits with bringing Buddhism to the Himalaya. The tenth day of the lunar month is linked to him.

For a village or a district, a tshechu is the biggest religious and social event of the year. Families walk in from distant farms, dressed in their best gho and kira, carrying lunch in baskets. They come to receive blessings by watching the dances, and also to meet relatives, gossip, and eat together on the grass. Most tshechus last about four days, and each day has its own set of dances. For visitors, it is a chance to see Bhutanese life at its most public, but it is a religious event first and a show second.

sections.heading: Cham dances, atsaras and the thongdrel
paras: The heart of a tshechu is the cham, the costumed and masked dances performed in the dzong courtyard. Many tell moral stories or episodes from Guru Rinpoche's life. Monks perform some group dances unmasked, including the Black Hat dance, while lay dancers perform the masked ones. The dancers train for weeks, and in Bhutan, registered festival dancers can be fined if they refuse to perform.

Between and during dances you will see the atsaras, masked clowns who wander through the crowd, tease people, and make fun of almost everything, including the dancers. They are part of the ritual, not a sideshow. If one picks you to joke with, smile and play along.

At many tshechus, the last morning brings the thongdrel, a huge appliqué thangka, usually showing Guru Rinpoche, unfurled on the dzong wall before dawn. At Paro, on the fifteenth day of the second lunar month, the thongdrel shows the Eight Manifestations of Guru Rinpoche, and tradition holds that sunlight should not fall on it, so it is rolled up by early morning. Bhutanese believe that seeing it brings great merit. To see it, you need to be in the courtyard well before first light.

sections.heading: The main festivals by month
paras: The table lists the festivals our travellers ask about most. Because they follow the Bhutanese lunar calendar, the Western dates move every year, sometimes by several weeks. Check the official festival calendar from the Department of Tourism for the year you travel before you book flights or hotels, and check current status before you travel.

Two festivals keep fixed Western dates, which makes them easy to plan around. The Black-necked Crane Festival is always on 11 November, and the Druk Wangyal Tshechu is held each 13 December at Dochula, the pass at about 3,100 m between Thimphu and Punakha, in front of the 108 chortens built by Queen Mother Ashi Dorji Wangmo Wangchuck. It is an open-air festival, so it can be very cold, but on a clear day the view of the high peaks to the north makes up for it.

sections.heading: What to wear
paras: Dress as you would for any dzong. That means long sleeves and long trousers or a long skirt, no shorts, and no caps or hats inside the dzong. Bhutanese wear their finest gho and kira to a tshechu, and a few visitors like to rent or buy a set for the day; locals usually take it as a compliment, and your guide can help you put it on. The ceremonial scarf, kabney for men and rachu for women, is worn by Bhutanese and is not expected of visitors.

Mornings in a stone courtyard are cold, especially at Paro in March and at Thimphu and Bumthang in October and November. Bring a warm layer you can keep on, a cushion or folded shawl to sit on, sunscreen, and water. Comfortable shoes matter: you may stand for an hour waiting for a good spot, and the stone steps can be uneven and crowded.

sections.heading: Seating, crowds and the dance ground
paras: The open space in the middle of the courtyard is the dance ground, and it is sacred for the duration of the festival. Never walk across it, even between dances, and never stand in it to take a photo. Atsaras and officials will move you if you do, and it is genuinely offensive.

Locals arrive early and sit on the steps, the galleries and the ground around the edge. Some areas are kept for monks, officials and guests; your guide will know which. Sit where you are shown, and do not save large spaces with bags. Keep your feet tucked in rather than pointing them toward the dancers or the altar. Big festivals such as Thimphu and Paro draw thousands of people, so be patient with the crowd and keep children close.

With children and older travellers, plan for shorter sessions. Two or three hours in the morning is plenty for most visitors; you can return to the hotel at lunch and come back for the late afternoon dances. Make sure everyone knows a meeting point outside the dzong gate in case you are separated in the crowd, and carry snacks, as stalls outside can have long queues.
list: Arrive by 8 am for a good spot on main days, and before dawn for the thongdrel.
Stay off the dance ground at all times.
Do not climb on walls, railings or the galleries for a better view.
Keep your voice low and your phone on silent.
Eat and drink quietly at the edges, as local families do, and take your rubbish with you.

sections.heading: Photography do's and don'ts
paras: Photography of the dances in the open courtyard is generally accepted, and you will see Bhutanese filming on their phones. The rules are about respect and space. Photography is not allowed inside temples and shrine rooms, festival or not. Ask your guide on the day, because individual dzongs and organisers can set their own rules.
list: Do: shoot from your seat, at the edge of the crowd.
Do: ask before photographing individual people up close, especially elders and monks.
Don't: use flash during dances or during the thongdrel.
Don't: step into the dance ground or block people sitting behind you.
Don't: set up tripods in crowded areas or fly a drone without official permission.

sections.heading: Booking hotels early
paras: Paro Tshechu and Thimphu Tshechu are the two busiest weeks of the tourist year. Certified 3-star hotels in Paro and Thimphu, normally ₹3,000–5,500 a room night with breakfast, can sell out months ahead, and rates rise. We suggest booking four to six months ahead for these two, and two to three months ahead for Punakha and the Black-necked Crane Festival, whose fixed date makes it easy to plan around. Indicative, 2026.

If Paro is full, stay in Thimphu, about 55 km and 1–1.5 hours away, and drive over early. Or skip the main day and see the dances on the first or second day, which are less crowded. Smaller village tshechus, which your guide may know about, can be the most rewarding of all: fewer visitors and closer to the dancers.

faqs.q: What is a tshechu festival in Bhutan
faqs.a: A tshechu is an annual religious festival held in a Bhutanese district on or around the tenth day of a lunar month, honouring Guru Rinpoche. Most last about four days and are held in a dzong or temple courtyard, with masked cham dances performed by monks and lay dancers. People come for blessings and to meet family. Many end with the unfurling of a giant thongdrel at dawn.

Paro Tshechu is held from the eleventh to the fifteenth day of the second month of the Bhutanese lunar calendar, which usually falls in March or April. The giant thongdrel is shown before dawn on the last day at Rinpung Dzong. Because the Western date changes every year, check the official Department of Tourism calendar before you book, and check current status before you travel.

Thimphu Tshechu usually falls in September or October, depending on the lunar calendar, and is held at Tashichho Dzong in Thimphu. It is the busiest festival of the year, so book hotels in Thimphu four to six months ahead. Check the official Department of Tourism festival calendar for the exact dates in the year you travel, and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can tourists attend tshechus in Bhutan
faqs.a: Yes. Tourists are welcome at tshechus and usually watch from the edges of the dzong courtyard with their licensed guide. Dress modestly with long sleeves and long trousers or a long skirt, remove hats, stay off the dance ground and avoid flash photography. Arrive early on the main days, as seats on the steps fill with local families by mid-morning.

faqs.q: Can I take photos at a Bhutan festival
faqs.a: Usually, yes, in the open courtyard during the dances, from your seat at the edge of the crowd. Do not use flash, do not step into the dance ground and do not block people behind you. Photography inside temples and shrine rooms is not allowed. Drones need official permission. Ask your guide on the day, as dzongs and organisers can set their own rules.

faqs.q: What should I wear to a tshechu
faqs.a: Wear what you would wear to a dzong: long sleeves, long trousers or a long skirt, closed shoes and no cap or hat inside. Bhutanese wear their best gho and kira, and some visitors rent or buy a set for the day, which locals usually appreciate. Bring a warm layer for cold mornings in the courtyard, and a cushion or shawl to sit on.

A thongdrel is a giant appliqué thangka, a religious image on cloth, unfurled on a dzong wall on the last morning of many tshechus. It usually shows Guru Rinpoche. At Paro, it shows his Eight Manifestations and is raised before dawn, then rolled up before sunlight falls on it, as tradition requires. Bhutanese believe seeing it brings great merit.

faqs.q: Who are the atsaras at Bhutanese festivals
faqs.a: Atsaras are the masked clowns of a tshechu. They move through the crowd during and between dances, joking with spectators, mimicking dancers and poking fun at almost everyone, and they also help keep people off the dance ground. They are part of the religious performance, not entertainment added for tourists. If an atsara jokes with you, smile and play along.

faqs.q: When is the Black-necked Crane Festival
faqs.a: The Black-necked Crane Festival is held every year on 11 November, the Fourth King's birthday, at Gangtey in the Phobjikha valley. It was started in 1998 by the Royal Society for Protection of Nature and celebrates the cranes that winter in the valley from late October to February or March. Because the date is fixed, it is easy to plan around; book Phobjikha hotels early.
